test: record GW-013 and cover a cleanly exiting child

Both found by mutation audit rather than by coverage. Forty mutations were
applied one at a time in a disposable copy and run against the whole suite;
a second, exhaustive pass enumerated 94 mutations mechanically over a fixed
operator set. Details and the full triage are in MCDC_REACHABILITY.md.

GW-013: both upstream-to-stdio bridges build their reply envelope with
`req.jsonrpc || '2.0'`, so a request declaring another version is answered
with that version. JSON-RPC 2.0 requires every response to carry "2.0"; a
request with jsonrpc 1.0 is answered {"jsonrpc":"1.0",...}. Two TODOs in
bridgeEnvelopeVersion.test.ts state the conformant envelope and are not
enabled, because asserting today's reply would bless the non-conformant one.
Replacing the whole expression with the constant '2.0' passes the entire
suite: every other test sends a conformant request, for which both forms
produce the same envelope, so the branch is covered and the statement is
asserted while nothing pins either.

The clean-exit gap is closed rather than recorded. Both gateways spell child
termination `process.exit(code ?? 1)`, and zero is the single exit code where
that differs from `code || 1`. Existing child-exit tests use 17, 19, 23 and a
null code for the signal case, so nothing verified that a child finishing
successfully leaves the gateway exiting 0 rather than 1, which is what a
supervisor, container runtime or CI step reads. childExitCodeZero.test.ts
covers both gateways and was confirmed to fail against the mutant.

After that fix, of the 66 measurable mutants in the exhaustive pass, 14 are
equivalent or near-equivalent and all 52 of the rest are killed. A further 28
mutations were rejected by tsc before any test ran.

stdioToSse.ts calls session.transport.send() with no await and no rejection

correct measurement of the current code, not a gap to close.

test: stop the lifecycle tests racing their own idle timeout

The first CI run failed two stateful tests with nothing but "test timed out
after 15000ms". Both configured a 300 ms idle timeout and then waited on the
peer to report; on a runner roughly twice as slow as a laptop, the session
expired in the gap between the initialize response and the held request
arriving, so the child was cleaned up and the peer never reported at all.

Reproduced by setting the idle timeout to 1 ms, which fails identically.

Two changes. The wait on the control server had no deadline, which is what
turned every such failure into an opaque timeout; it now rejects after 10s
naming the likely cause, leaving the test its own budget to report in. And the
three 300 ms idle timeouts become 1000 ms with their paired waits kept at twice
the timeout, so the assertions still prove that active work survives past
expiry, with margin for a slower machine.

test: record GW-015 and retain its two reproducers as opt-in TODOs

CI's named deadline pointed both failures at the same step: the child is never
released when a stateful session ends, by idle expiry or by explicit DELETE.

Reproduced in a node:24 container and traced to the spawn/kill pair every
gateway uses. Children start under `spawn(cmd, { shell: true })` and stop with
`child.kill()`. macOS runs bash as sh, which execs, so child.pid is the server
and the signal lands. Linux runs dash, which forks, so child.pid is the shell
and the server survives as a grandchild:

  spawned child.pid = 14        (dash)
  matching processes: 14, 15    (15 is the real node server)
  child.kill() -> shell gone, 15 still running

That makes it a production defect on the platform the Docker image ships to,
where every ended session leaves its MCP server process behind. It stayed
invisible because the suite had only ever run on macOS.

No production change here, per the current split: the two tests become GW-015
reproducers under the existing opt-in convention, so the default suite is green
on Linux (115 passed, 0 failed, 29 TODO, verified in the container) and the
guardrail can merge. They only fail on Linux, so the findings note gives a
container command rather than a bare RUN_KNOWN_BUG_TESTS line.

Four detectors, each aimed at a class the existing suite structurally cannot
see. Every one is justified by a defect already in this repository.

Lint. `no-floating-promises` finds GW-004 and GW-014 in ten seconds without a
test, a reproducer or a matrix, plus three `transport.close()` calls nobody had
noticed. `no-misused-promises` finds the async handlers assigned to void
callback slots, which is how a thrown TypeError becomes an unhandled rejection
rather than a caught error. `require-await` was tried and dropped: seven
findings, all gateway entry points that are async for API shape, no defects.

Leak budget. A root `afterEach`, loaded through --import, runs after every test
and before its own t.after cleanup, so gateways are still alive and their
descendants can be counted. It catches accumulation — #108's child-per-POST, the
orphans in #141 and #160 — and deliberately not GW-015's single straggler, which
the harness's group kill makes indistinguishable from teardown.

A second client. Nothing in 55 test files opened two clients against one
gateway, which is how #112, #138 and #153 stayed open: every test exercises each
gateway once, and a bug needing a *second* connection is invisible however well
the first is covered.

An SDK matrix. The lockfile pins 1.18.2 while `^1.18.2` lets consumers resolve
up to 1.30.0, twenty-six releases later. The two-client test passes on the pin
and fails on 1.30.0 — so cluster C exists only on the SDK users actually get,
and no test written against the lockfile could ever have found it. One job per
minor line, so a failure also names the release that introduced it.

Lint and the SDK matrix are advisory: both are expected to be red across part of
their range until the bugs they found are fixed, and that map is the point.

test: fix two sources of flakiness in the harness

Both surfaced while adding the property tests, and both are almost certainly the
unidentified flake recorded earlier in TODO.md.

kill EPERM. Cleanup signals the gateway's process group and tolerated ESRCH but
not EPERM. A gateway that was supposed to exit on its own leaves a group that is
gone, and if the pid has since been recycled into a group we do not own the
signal fails with EPERM rather than ESRCH. Neither means the test failed.

Port re-issue. unusedPort binds port 0, reads the number and closes, which
leaves a window for the OS to hand the same port to something else; with 55
files churning the ephemeral range it does. The loser never binds and the test
fails eight seconds later saying only that the gateway "did not become ready",
which is why this was hard to place. The allocator now remembers what it has
issued and will not hand the same port out twice in a run.

Three consecutive full runs are clean at 118 passing, against two failures in
the two runs before the fixes.

fix: build against the whole declared SDK range

`^1.18.2` claims support up to 1.30.0 while the lockfile pinned 1.18.2, and the
source did not compile against most of what it claimed. Three causes, and only
one was ours.

zod. SDK 1.24 types its schema parameter as `z3.ZodTypeAny | z4.$ZodType`,
imported through the `zod/v3` subpath, and requires `zod: ^3.25 || ^4.0`. We
declared ^3.24.4, which has no such subpath, so `request(req, z.any())` produced
TS2345 and TS2589 in both reverse bridges. Bumping to ^3.25.76 clears both with
no source change — they were never a code problem.

protocolVersion. From 1.22 `params` is a union of every request shape and only
the initialize member carries protocolVersion, so the assignment in
streamableHttpToStdio stopped type-checking. The safeParse guard above it
already establishes that this is an initialize request and that its params are
present, so the cast records what the guard proved. Typed `unknown` because the
source field is `{}` on 1.18 and `string` on 1.30. Left as a plain assignment
rather than the SSE bridge's read-then-overwrite, which would have changed
behaviour: this bridge sets the version whether or not the request carried one.

skipLibCheck. 1.21 ships a declaration importing @cfworker/json-schema, which is
a peer rather than a dependency, so tsc failed on the SDK's own types. Worth
reporting upstream; skipping lib checks is the workaround and was arguably
missing anyway.

The result is that the matrix now measures behaviour instead of a build.
1.22.0, 1.24.3 and 1.30.0 all compile, and 1.30.0 reports 114 passing with four
real failures: three streamableHttp bridge tests and the two-client test.

Also adds step-level timeouts, which bound a hung run even on Node 18 where
--test-timeout does not exist.

fix: stop forwarding HTTP status codes as JSON-RPC error codes (GW-016)

Both reverse bridges answered a failed upstream request by copying whatever
`err.code` the transport carried straight onto the wire. That was harmless while
the SDK threw a plain Error for a failed POST, and wrong from 1.24, where it
throws StreamableHTTPError carrying the HTTP status — so clients started
receiving `{"error":{"code":503}}` and `{"code":400}`. JSON-RPC reserves
-32768..-32000 for protocol errors and no client can interpret a 503 there.

The code is now forwarded only when it falls in that reserved range, which every
McpError code does, and anything else becomes -32000. The discarded status is
not lost: older SDKs spelled it into the message themselves and newer ones only
carry it in the code, so it is prefixed as `HTTP <status>` when the message does
not already contain it.

This was always wrong, independent of any SDK version — the bug was latent
rather than absent below 1.24, which is why those columns were green.

Measured across the range: 1.18.2 118 passing 0 failing, 1.24.3 118/0, 1.26.0
116/2, 1.30.0 117/1. The three streamableHttp bridge failures are gone
everywhere. What remains is the second-client test, which is cluster C, and one
malformed-envelope test that fails on 1.26 but not 1.30 and is still undiagnosed.

test: mark the malformed-envelope check as an expected upstream failure

SDK 1.25.3 and 1.26.0 answer 200 to a malformed envelope they should reject with
400; 1.24.3 rejects it and 1.27.1 rejects it again. The regression is the SDK's
and it fixed it itself.

Neither obvious response was right. Teaching the test to expect 200 on those two
releases would put someone else's regression in our suite permanently, and
skipping it would drop the check on every version, including the ones where it
is the only thing asserting that behaviour.

So the check runs everywhere, and on the affected band it is declared an
expected upstream failure. Unlike a skip or a TODO the expectation is enforced
both ways: on an affected version the test must still fail, and if it starts
passing the marker fails loudly, naming the SDK version and saying that either
the dependency is fixed, the range is wrong, or the fault was never upstream.
Verified by widening the band over a version where the test passes.

Only for defects in a dependency. A test failing because this gateway is wrong
belongs in knownBugTest, or gets fixed — GW-016 was the latter.

Measured: 1.24.3 118 passing 0 failing with the marker inactive, 1.26.0 117/1
with it active, 1.27.1 117/1 with it inactive again. The single remaining
failure from 1.25 upward is cluster C.

test: hold the SSE client-isolation defect as a TODO (GW-017)

A reply to one SSE client is delivered to every connected client. The gateway
runs one child and one Server, and fans every child message out to every entry
in its session map, so nothing routes a reply back to the session that asked.

The test reads raw SSE frames rather than driving an SDK client, because the
client pairs each reply with its request and would discard a misrouted one
before an assertion could see it. Only one of the two sessions sends anything;
the other must not see the answer.

It fails on every SDK we support, for two different reasons, and both are worth
keeping visible:

  - below 1.25 the bystander receives the reply, and the isolation assertion
    fires;
  - from 1.25 the SDK refuses the second server.connect() with 'Already
    connected to a transport' and the test fails in about a second on a closed
    socket. That guard is the fix for GHSA-345p-7cg4-v4c7, cross-client data
    leak via shared server/transport instance reuse, which is this defect.

So the reports in #112, #138 and #153 describe the guard, not the cause.
Multi-client was never isolated; newer SDKs stopped letting it happen quietly.

TODO by default, opt in with RUN_KNOWN_BUG_TESTS=1. No production code is
changed here — this is the spec the fix has to satisfy, written before the fix.

test: pin the ordering that stops a dropped client killing the gateway

stdioToSse fans every child message out to every session without awaiting the
send and without a rejection handler. SSEServerTransport.send is async, so a
delivery to a transport whose response is gone rejects instead of throwing, and
nothing in src/ installs an unhandledRejection handler — Node terminates. The
only reason that never fires is that the close handler removes the session
before the next fan-out reaches it.

That is load-bearing and nowhere stated. Verified by mutation: delete the three
session removals from the compiled gateway and this test fails with 'the gateway
must still be running after a client disappears' — the process is gone, not
merely erroring. One vanished client would take every unrelated client with it.

Pinned now because fixing GW-017 rewrites this exact code — how replies reach
sessions — and this is the failure mode that refactor can silently reintroduce.
The test asserts the gateway survives, still answers the client that stayed, and
still accepts a new one, so it fails on death and on wedging alike.

Passes today. No production code changed.

test: hold the two-client test as GW-017 rather than enforce it

This test passed on SDK ≤1.25.3 and failed from 1.26.0, and it was the only
thing keeping the SDK matrix red. Marking it held is not a convenience: its
green was the misleading kind.

It asserts that two clients both reach the upstream server. That is not the
property that matters — both reaching it without seeing each other's traffic
is. The versions where it passed are exactly the versions that do not guard the
shared-instance reuse in GHSA-345p-7cg4-v4c7, so the second client was served
by leaking, and a green column certified the vulnerable configuration as
working. From 1.26.0 the SDK refuses the second connect, which is the same
defect seen from the other side.

sseClientIsolation.test.ts asserts what this one should have. This stays as the
reachability half of GW-017: when the fix lands, both are enabled together and
both must pass.

test: separate surviving a dropped client from reconnecting after one

The survival test connected two clients, which is GW-017's other half, so it
could not run at all from SDK 1.26 up — it failed at the second connection
rather than at anything it was asserting. Rewritten to use one client: the
delayed tool holds the reply while the socket is aborted, so the fan-out is
guaranteed to land after the disconnect, which is the window that matters. It
now passes on 1.18.2 and on 1.30.0.

Liveness is probed with a request to an unknown session rather than a second
/sse connection, for the same reason. It also has to be a round trip: the
fan-out is logged before the send is attempted, so asserting exitCode straight
after the log races a process that is about to die — verified, the mutation
stopped being caught until the probe went back in.

Still load-bearing: remove the session cleanup from the compiled gateway and it
fails with 'a dropped client took the whole process down'.

The reconnection case it used to smuggle in is now its own held test, because

fix: relay client notifications upstream instead of echoing them back

Manual testing of the published 4.0.0-rc.1 against a real server found two
defects that six hours of soak across twelve platforms did not.

Both stdio bridges classified a stdin frame as request-or-not, and wrote
everything that was not a request to stdout — the direction it had just
arrived from. So a client's `notifications/initialized` came straight back
to that client, and never reached the server. MCP Inspector shows a
`SERVER → CLIENT notifications/initialized` on every single connection
because of it, and a server sending that notification is not something the
protocol allows. The same path returned a client's response to a
server-initiated request back to the client, leaving the server waiting,
and dropped `notifications/cancelled` so a server kept working on requests
its client had abandoned.

Notifications and responses now go upstream. `notifications/initialized`
is the exception: `Client.connect` sends its own as the last step of the
handshake, so relaying the client's copy would deliver a second one to a
server that has already seen it. A relay failure is logged rather than
thrown, because the client is still connected and its next request
deserves an answer.

Three existing tests had pinned the old behaviour, one of them describing
it as passing frames "straight through". They now assert the frame reaches
the server and that nothing is echoed back.

Also give a stateful session a default idle timeout of thirty minutes. A
session owns a child process and the only thing that released it was the
client explicitly deleting the session; a client that crashes, is
force-quit, or just closes its transport never sends that, so every such
disconnect stranded a process for the lifetime of the gateway. Measured
2 -> 5 children over three connect/disconnect cycles. Thirty minutes is far
longer than any gap between calls in a live session and still bounds what a
vanished client can leave behind.

fix: answer 404 for a session id the stateful gateway no longer holds

Stateful stdio→Streamable HTTP collapsed two different faults into one 400:
a request with no `Mcp-Session-Id` header at all, and a request carrying a
session id the gateway does not hold. Only the first is a 400.

The Streamable HTTP spec makes the second a 404, and that 404 is the only
signal a compliant client gets that it should re-initialize:

  "The server MAY terminate the session at any time, after which it MUST
   respond to requests containing that session ID with HTTP 404 Not Found.
   When a client receives HTTP 404 in response to a request containing an
   Mcp-Session-Id, it MUST start a new session by sending a new
   InitializeRequest without a session ID attached."

Answering 400 leaves the client replaying a dead id until a human restarts
it. A client reaches that state after `--sessionTimeout` reaps an idle
session, after an explicit DELETE, and across a gateway restart.

The status codes themselves are unchanged since 3.4.3, so this is not a
regression — but 4.0.0 is the release that makes the path ordinary. Stateful
sessions now default to a 30-minute idle timeout (added with the child-leak
fix); before that, an unconfigured gateway never terminated a session, so the
branch was close to unreachable in practice. Every idle session now expires.

Both handlers are covered: the POST chain gains an unknown-session branch
returning 404 with JSON-RPC -32001, and the shared GET/DELETE handler splits
its `!sessionId || !transports.has(sessionId)` guard so a missing header keeps

tool call failed with "Request timed out" even when the client would wait.
Measured: a 65-second tool, client timeout 120s, failed after 60s through both
bridges; it now completes. The client owns the deadline, and when it gives up
its cancellation now arrives.

fix: a WebSocket client's cancel reaches the request it named

Requests reach the child with their id tunnelled as `<clientId>:<id>`, but a
client's notifications/cancelled went through unchanged, naming an id the child
had never seen, so cancelling over WebSocket did nothing and the tool ran on.
The cancel's requestId is now tunnelled the same way.

Also drop the transport's console.log of every client notification: it
bypassed --logLevel (printing even with `none`), and the gateway already logs
that traffic through its logger.

fix: answer a rejected HTTP body as JSON-RPC, not an HTML stack trace

Invalid JSON, an unsupported charset or a body over 4 MB reached Express's
default error handler in both Streamable HTTP modes. A client got an HTML page
it could not parse, and unless NODE_ENV was `production` the page carried the
stack trace with the server's absolute file paths. They are now JSON-RPC
errors with the same status codes: 400 with a -32700 parse error for invalid
JSON, 415 and 413 with -32000 for the others.

fix: a --baseUrl with a trailing slash no longer breaks SSE clients

The endpoint was `${baseUrl}${messagePath}` joined as text, so
`--baseUrl https://host/gateway/` gave `/gateway//message`, and a bare origin
with its slash, `--baseUrl http://localhost:8000/`, gave `//message`. A client
reads that as a protocol-relative URL, `http://message/?sessionId=…`, so every
POST went to a host named "message". Trailing slashes are dropped before the
join.

fix: route path flags given without a leading slash

Express only matches routes that start with `/`, so `--ssePath sse`,
`--messagePath message`, `--streamableHttpPath mcp` or `--healthEndpoint
health` registered a route no request could reach. Every request got a 404,
with no warning, and the startup log printed `http://localhost:8000sse`. The
slash is now added when the flags are parsed; paths that already start with
one are unchanged.

test: keep the pre-connect relay covered now that bridges handle cancels

A cancel no longer reaches the relay (the bridge handles it), so the
pre-connect frame in bridgeInputShapes is a roots/list_changed notification
instead. And a request found by its requestId implies the params were there,
so the reason lookup no longer carries a nullish branch nothing can reach.

fix: give each WebSocket connection its own child

All WebSocket clients shared one child. Replies were routed by rewriting each
request id to `<clientId>:<id>`, but notifications and the server's own
requests carry no client id, so they were broadcast: client B received client
A's log messages and progress (measured: B, which never sent anything, got all
six), and B could be asked to answer A's sampling request. The id rewriting
also caused GW-018 and the broken server requests and cancellation fixed
earlier.

Each connection now spawns its own child, as each SSE connection has since
#221, and messages pass through unchanged. The transport becomes a per-client
socket registry. Consequences, as with #221:
- a child exiting closes its own client's socket (1011, with the reason), and
  the gateway stays up instead of exiting with the child's code;
- a child is spawned when a client connects, not at startup, and one that
  cannot start refuses that connection;
- the health endpoint reports the gateway, not a process-wide child.

fix: the SSE bridge's stream request keeps the SDK's headers

The bridge wraps the event source's fetch to add --header values, merging them
with `{ ...init.headers, ...headers }`. The SDK passes a `Headers` object, and
spreading one yields `{}`, so the stream request lost every header the SDK set:
it went out as `Accept: */*` instead of `text/event-stream`, and without
`mcp-protocol-version`. A server that checks Accept refuses the stream. The
headers are now merged, and a configured header still wins.

fix: reject a non-numeric --sessionTimeout instead of disabling it

`--sessionTimeout 30m` parses as NaN, which passed the `<= 0` check, so the
gateway started with "Session timeout: disabled": the 30-minute default that
stops a vanished client leaking its child was silently switched off. It is now
rejected like 0 and negative values.

perf: read child stdout in linear time

All five stdout readers did `buffer += chunk; buffer.split(/\r?\n/)`, rescanning
everything held on every chunk, so a line arriving in many chunks cost time
proportional to its length squared. Measured through stateful HTTP, one reply
of: 5 MB 0.04s, 20 MB 0.39s, 50 MB 2.30s. They now share a LineSplitter that
searches only the new text for a newline and joins a held line once: 5 MB
0.03s, 20 MB 0.10s, 50 MB 0.25s, 100 MB 0.42s. Framing is unchanged: lines end
at LF with one CR before it dropped, as the regex split did.

fix: stateless children speak the protocol version the client negotiated

Stateless mode gives every request a fresh child and initializes it itself,
always with --protocolVersion (default 2024-11-05). So a client that negotiated
2025-11-25 had every request after initialize served by a child that believed
it was talking to a 2024-11-05 client, and a server can withhold newer features
from such a client. Measured with the SDK client: negotiated 2025-11-25, each
tools/call reached a child initialized with 2024-11-05.

From 2025-06-18 on, a client names its version in every request's
MCP-Protocol-Version header, and the SDK has already refused a version it does
not support. The child now gets that version; --protocolVersion applies only to
a request that names none.

fix: --header reaches every Streamable HTTP response, not only health

In SSE mode --header set headers on every response. In both Streamable HTTP
modes it was applied only in the health handler, so the MCP responses a client
or proxy sees never carried it (measured: present on /health, absent on the
initialize response). It is now set in the first middleware, so every
response gets it, including JSON-RPC body errors. The README lists the mode.

stateless HTTP, and WebSocket's server) now keeps them for 65, so the other

minutes, and a client's close() does not end the session). Measured: 30
